blocks.text: It seems rather to be the sturnus [starling].

This, however, is exactly what J. E. Faber did in his dissertation de Animalibus, quorum mentio sit Zephan. II, 14 (Göttingen 1769; reprinted at the end of Cramer's book entitled Scythische Denkmaeler in Palaestina), where he contends that قيق [qyq], قوق [qwq], ܩܩܐ, קיק, קוק, קקא and קקתא are names of a single bird, the cornix [crow], differing from one another only in spelling. But even if the Hebrew masters sometimes take קוק and קיק indiscriminately for the crow, it is nevertheless clear from what Bochart has adduced from Damir that the Arabic قيق [qyq] and قوق [qwq] differ from each other; and that the Syriac ܩܩܐ designates the pelican is clearly taught by the Physiologus Syrus edited by Tychsen, ch. 20, pp. 13 and 110, and by Tychsen himself, pp. 111–114. The Syriac name of the crow is rather ܩܘܪܩܣܐ Korakso, which arose from the sound and is the Greek κόραξ [korax]; see the same Physiolog. Syr. Chapter 24. Faber, therefore, interprets the Hebrew word as the crow on the authority of the Arabic translator in the Polyglots alone, who puts قيق [qyq] for קאת. Schoder copied Faber in Specim. Hieroz. II, Tit. 9. But in truth the crow in no way fits the passages of the Psalms and Zephaniah. For Zephaniah II, 14 places the קאת among the ruins and deserted places of the cities of Nineveh and Zion, whereas the crow frequents the surroundings of cities and houses; and David, Psalm. CII, 7, compares his weeping with the laments and groans of the קאת; yet no one, so far as I know, has ever yet heard laments from a crow. Moreover, Moses in Levit. XI, 18 has already included the crow under the genus of ravens, ערב, so that there was no need to name this bird separately, as Oedmann aptly points out, fasc. 3, Chapter 6, p. 58.

Add what our author will discuss below, book 4, ch. 27, p. 623. That the Hebrew קיקיון, the Arabic الخروع [al-khirwaʿ], and the Egyptian Kiki is the ricinus vulgaris or medicus, French Palme de Christ, German der Wunderbaum, is shown by Celsius in Hierobot. vol. 2, pp. 273–282, and Michaelis in Supplemm. vol. 6, p. 2185 ff. Compare Niebuhr's Descript. Arab. p. 148 and Forsskål's Flora Aegyptio-Arabica, pp. 164, 75, 121.

To Michaelis, in Supplemm. ad Lexx. Hebrr. vol. 6, p. 2158, the letter ת does not seem to be a feminine ending but part of the root; for from the root קיא, to vomit, one could indeed form קאה, but not קאת. But Michaelis did not consider that the word קאת must be derived from קאה, to vomit out, which occurs in Levit. XVIII, 28, and that there are some nouns derived from verbs with quiescent third He which usually take the letter Thau in the place and function of the third radical, such as the nouns Bochart listed above, to which may be added שפת, lip, דלת, door, קשת, bow, from שפה, דלה, קשה, etc. Cf. Schroeder, Institt. ad fundamenta Ling. Hebr. sect. 7, rule 106 β, p. 135.

He means the Platalea Leucorodia of Linnaeus (Syst. Nat. vol. 1, part 2, p. 613, ed. Gmelin). But what the ancients relate in their tales about their πελεκανος [pelekanos] does not fit the Platalea: that this bird loves its young so much that, whenever food is lacking, it wounds its own breast with its beak so that they may not die of hunger, and gives them the flowing blood to drink. How the Platalea could wound itself with its broad bill is hard to understand. J. D. Michaelis, in the Quaestiones proposed to those travelling to Arabia, no. 100, p. 331, in the Nott. ad Vernacul. on Levit. XI, and in Supplemm. ad Lexx. Hebrr. vol. 6, p. 2158, takes the πελεκαν [pelekan] of the ancient authors for the onocrotalus of the moderns. But Oedmann rightly points out, fasc. 3, p. 60, that for the ancients themselves the onocrotalus and the pelican are different birds (see also our author above, Chapter 20, p. 275), whereas everything the ancients relate about the pelican is found in the Pelecanus Graculus of Linnaeus (Syst. vol. 1, part 2, p. 574), of which he also added a picture.
That the Pelecanus Graculus also vomits up fish was observed by Georgi, cited by Oedmann (3, p. 61).
By the heron Bochart means the stellaris, called Butor by the French, Bittour or Bittern by the English, Rohrdommel by the Germans. See Linnaeus, Syst. vol. 1, part 2, p. 635 f.
And in Aldrovandi, Ornithol. vol. 3, book 20, Chapter 16, p. 403, from Gesner.
